items.title: Shutting the Door on the XCPE Botnet
items.summary: Google and partners dismantled the XCPE backdoor, which was built into set-top boxes and enrolled over 1.3 million devices in a botnet. The backdoor was deliberately created by the Android manufacturer Videostrong, which sold access to criminal affiliates for ad fraud, residential proxying and malware delivery. The manufacturer evaded Google's compatibility tests by loading malicious code after first boot.
items.takeaway: Vetting a device or software at build or certification time does not prove what it does after first boot, so supply chain assurance needs runtime monitoring and egress visibility.

items.title: What Standard Evaluations Hide About Detectors of Hijacked LLM Agents: Rare Attacks, Unseen Tools and Benchmark Transfer
items.summary: The authors audited eleven evaluations of detectors for hijacked LLM agents and found that attack rates in test sets ranged from 16% to 86%, with none varying that share. At a realistic 2% attack rate, a detector with an AUROC of 0.879 had a precision of only 0.076, and detector rankings reversed when tools unseen in training made up more than half of test calls. Detectors trained on one benchmark scored near chance on another, and the authors close with a checklist for evaluating trace detectors.
items.takeaway: A high AUROC can hide poor real-world alert quality, because precision collapses when attacks are rare, so evaluate detectors at deployment base rates and on unseen tools or sources.

items.title: What exploited vulnerabilities have in common: A data-driven analysis of real-world attacks
items.summary: Microsoft analyses the vulnerability landscape, noting that only about 0.5% of roughly 383,000 disclosed CVEs have been linked to real-world exploitation. Attackers focus on flaws enabling system takeover, especially remote code execution, privilege escalation and authentication bypass. The post argues that AI-assisted discovery could shorten defenders' response windows, so protection should target both exploitation likelihood and potential blast radius.
items.takeaway: Prioritise remediation by combining the likelihood of exploitation with the blast radius of compromise, since most CVEs are never exploited in the wild.

items.title: The Rise of LLMJacking: How Threat Actors Monetize Compromised Cloud and Model Resources
items.summary: Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence describe LLMJacking intrusions in 2026, where attackers hijack enterprise LLM API access and generate fraudulent charges that can exceed $100,000 in a day. They also describe a division of labour in which initial access brokers hand off to LLM Mixers that resell unauthorised model access to underground subscribers.
items.takeaway: Cloud AI API spend is a security signal: alert on sudden spikes in token or request volume, since this abuse can cost far more in hours than cryptojacking does over weeks.

items.title: Backporting security fixes at scale with Codex
items.summary: Trail of Bits describes using Codex agents to cut the time needed to backport security fixes to older Linux kernel, Ubuntu and Fedora releases from days to hours. The workflow has helped deliver fixes for 149 CVEs into stable kernel releases, with agents doing the adaptation and testing while engineers review and submit patches. The authors stress that regression testing and maintainer acceptance remain essential.
items.takeaway: Agents work best on well-scoped, verifiable steps such as adapting patches and assembling test evidence, with human reviewers keeping responsibility for the final decision.

items.title: SecPO: Principled Adversarial Training for Prompt Injection Security
items.summary: The authors argue that Meta-SecAlign's DPO-based training anchors the model to an insecure reference, and that adversarial training on weak simulated attacks leaves it exposed. They propose a SecPO loss that approximates an injection-invariant reference, combined with a stronger adversarial training pipeline. The result cuts attack success rates on adaptive prompt injections by large factors while keeping benign utility across nine benchmarks.
items.takeaway: Defences against prompt injection are only as good as the attacks used to train them, so evaluate with adaptive attackers that optimise against your specific defence, not fixed benchmark payloads.

items.title: When AI Investigators Cannot Trust Their Tools: Conflict-Aware Evidence Verification for Cyber Threat Investigation
items.summary: The paper shows that LLM-based alert triage collapses when the detection tools feeding it are partly corrupted, with unverified investigators falling to as low as 0.13 accuracy. The proposed Conflict-Aware Evidence Verification adds an equal-weight vote, a conflict gate and an independent nearest-neighbour trust check, recovering accuracy to 0.84 to 0.88 while calling the LLM on only 0.4% of clean traffic. The authors also show that the verification channel itself becomes a target that must be measured and protected.
items.takeaway: When an automated investigator consumes machine-generated evidence, trust should be moved to an independent, monitored verification step rather than assumed in each tool. Any such check is itself an attack surface and needs its own testing.

items.title: CARI: Cross-Boundary Adversarial Runtime Injection in Coding-Agent Workflows
items.summary: The authors introduce CARI, an attack where a malicious peer-controlled component, such as a backend service or CI job, embeds instructions in runtime diagnostic feedback that a victim coding agent then acts on. It succeeds in 94.8% of 3,000 trials across models and transfers to Codex (61.3%) and Claude Code (58.7%), and generic prompt warnings either fail or cause over-refusal.
items.takeaway: Trust should follow the authority a source holds over an action, not just whether it is a legitimate data channel, because diagnostic output from a component that cannot act can still steer an agent that can.

items.title: Security Impact of Coding Agent's Memory Files
items.summary: The study examines coding agent memory files such as CLAUDE.md, which are loaded as trusted guidance and can be changed through a pull request. Malicious files shifted secure-completion rates by only -8 to +6 points, but agents differed sharply in whether they disclosed the file's influence, and flagging it as an attack did not stop vulnerable code.
items.takeaway: Agent configuration files are a supply chain attack surface that should be reviewed like code, and warning the model about them is not a reliable control.

items.title: Beyond Smart Homes: Characterizing IoT Vulnerabilities Across Sectors, Vendors, and Products
items.summary: The authors analyse over 15,000 IoT-specific CVEs, using lexical matching, fuzzy clustering and LLM-assisted classification to normalise vendor and product metadata and label sectors. They find that weakness profiles differ by sector, with healthcare dominated by authentication and credential flaws and automotive by memory issues. They also find that products from the same vendor share weakness profiles more than products of the same type from different vendors.
items.takeaway: Vendor-level practices such as shared code and development habits strongly shape which weaknesses appear, so a vendor's past disclosure history can help predict risk in its other products. Remediation priorities should therefore follow weakness classes rather than uniform aggregate guidance.

items.title: How Much Can Tool Calls Reveal About You? Privacy Leakage from Tool-Call Traces
items.summary: The paper introduces PrivacyTrace, a benchmark of synthetic user profiles and agent trajectories built on real MCP tools, to test whether tool-call traces reveal user attributes. Four LLM attackers inferred profile attributes at a 26.25% success rate, versus 17.97% from prior-based guessing alone. Tool arguments and returned results carried most of the leaked signal, and linking traces across sessions made profiling worse.
items.takeaway: Metadata from agent tool use, such as arguments and results logged across sessions, is a privacy side channel even when conversations are never exposed, so apply minimisation and retention limits to traces.

items.title: LanG 2.0: Energy-Efficient Agentic AI for Semi-Automated Security Operations at Scale
items.summary: LanG 2.0 is an agentic SOC system that correlates alerts and flows, writes detection rules, and uses small local models. It adds entity-anchored correlation, human approval of rule changes, and a tamper-evident ledger, reporting large gains in campaign precision and rule acceptance, along with much lower energy use than a frontier model and resistance to prompt injection and label poisoning.
items.takeaway: When deploying LLMs in detection workflows, rely on structural controls such as human approval gates and tamper-evident logs for guarantees, rather than assuming a more accurate model will make the system safe.

items.title: MetaVul: Agentic Harness Discovery for Vulnerability Detection
items.summary: The authors present MetaVul, which uses a workflow-based optimisation loop to automatically refine the scaffolding (harness) around an LLM for pairwise vulnerability detection, learning from paired vulnerable and patched functions. The optimised harnesses improve accuracy by up to 25.8 points on a held-out set, and harnesses tuned on one model transfer to others without further optimisation.
items.takeaway: In LLM-based detection, the scaffolding around the model can matter as much as the model itself, so evaluate tooling and prompts with paired vulnerable and patched code to separate real security signal from benign variation.

items.title: DeepWeave: Weaving Neural and Symbolic Evidence for ML-Based Network Intrusion Detection System
items.summary: DeepWeave is a neuro-symbolic network intrusion detection system that combines automatically learned interpretable rules with neural predictions treated as probabilistic predicates. With only 50 labelled packet observations per attack class, it raised macro-F1 from 0.632 to 0.924 and cut the attack false-positive rate from 0.075 to 0.008 compared with a matched neural baseline. The authors also report that its proofs were more stable than post-hoc neural attributions.
items.takeaway: Pairing a learned classifier with explicit, checkable rules can give analysts alert explanations that are more stable than post-hoc attributions, and can help when labelled attack data is scarce.

items.title: When Safety Checks Become Privacy Risks: A Privacy-Preserving Paradigm for LLM Agent Safety Auditing
items.summary: The paper argues that sending tool-call details to an external safety auditor for LLM agents can leak sensitive user data, and proposes separating trusted representation, encrypted audit computation and execution control. The SealCall prototype uses learned representations and CKKS homomorphic encryption to compare audit inputs without exposing plaintext to a semi-honest auditor. It reached a mean F1 of 0.840 on 1,252 binary candidates, with each encrypted scoring operation taking about 0.176 seconds.
items.takeaway: Security monitoring of sensitive workloads can be outsourced without exposing the data by encrypting the audit computation and binding the enforcement decision to the audited action.
